newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. refugee chief blasts Rwanda on refugees in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. refugee chief blasts Rwanda on refugees in Zaire.

text.p: Sadako Ogata, the U.N High Commissioner for Refugees, on Wednesday blasted Rwanda for accusing her of blocking repatriation of refugees from eastern Zaire and mismanaging a weekend train tragedy.

"The charges leveled by the Rwandan government and the (rebels) against the humanitarian relief effort in eastern Zaire are outrageous, unfair and demonstrably false," she said in a letter to Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu.

Kigali twice this month, in letters to Ogata, charged that UNHCR was blocking repatriation of Rwandan refugees. It said the agency was responsible for the deaths of 92 refugees in a packed train taking them from Biaro to Kisangani on Sunday.

Ogata, according to a statement, said the dispatch of the train was not cleared with U.N. agencies. The deaths were the result of refugees rushing to board after an attack by local Zairean villagers, according to witnesses.

The recent conflict again highlights friction between U.N. agencies and the Zairean rebels, led by Laurent Kabila's Alliance for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, with participation from Rwanda. With alliance forces closing around the capital of Kinshasa, the treatment of the refugees, including reports of massacres, has tarnished Kabila's international reputation in the U.N. Security Council and elsehwere.

Ogata, currently in New York, welcomed a call from Rwanda for an independent international inquiry into how refugees were being treated in Zaire, according to a statement. But she said such a probe should cover not only the train tragedy but recent attacks on refugee camps.
"The refugees continue to face major human rights violations and even summary execution," she said.

Soren Jessen-Petersen, the New York director of UNHCR, told a news conference it was "absolutely unacceptable" that Rwanda carry out a threat to repatriate the refugees directly without international help.

"Attempts to run this on a bilateral basis might be a cover for some more sinister schemes," he said, adding, however, that Rwanda had treated the refugees well on their return. UNHCR, he said, had the ability to do the job if they were allowed access.
He said refugees were drifting back to camps because "they hear that we are back," adding: "Going back (home) is better than certain death in and around Kisangani" in Zaire.

Jessen-Petersen said UNHCR also was very worried about "hate radio" broadcasts in eastern Zaire inciting local villages against the Rwandan refugees as well as U.N. relief groups. He said he did not know who was financing them.

The Rwandan Hutu refugees are part of more than a million Hutus who fled to Zaire in 1994 to escape reprisals for the genocide of Tutsis, who now run the Kigali government. They were driven deeper into the countryside when the Tutsi-dominated rebels launched an offensive.

Many have gone home but close to 300,000 are still believed to be in Zaire, with around 40,000 recently drifting back to camps for an airlift home. Some, including Hutu fighters, are in the West near the Republic of Congo and others are drifting toward Angola in the southwest.
